passages.happening:
“In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of the Danites was looking for territory to occupy” (verse 1). Dan sends five men from Zorah and Eshtaol to explore the land (verse 2).

In the hill country of Ephraim they stay at Micah's house and recognize the voice of the young Levite. They ask what he is doing there, and he tells them Micah has hired him as his priest (verses 3-4). They ask him to inquire of God whether their way will succeed. “Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey” (verses 5-6).

The five men come to Laish, in the far north. Its people live ‘securely, like the Sidonians, tranquil and unsuspecting’. They lack nothing, they have no harsh ruler, and they have no alliance with anyone (verse 7).

They go home and tell their brothers to attack: “When you enter, you will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land, for God has delivered it into your hand” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The tribe of Dan had been given land in the low hills west of Benjamin and Judah, around Zorah and Eshtaol. But it could not hold it. Chapter 1 told how the Amorites pushed it back into the hills, and later the Philistines pressed on it, as in the days of Samson. Now Dan goes looking for a new home.

The scouts recall the spies Moses sent into Canaan, and the two Joshua sent to Jericho. Sending spies was ordinary in ancient war, and so was asking for a word from God before a venture. But the Danites do not ask God themselves. They ask a hired priest, and his answer is vague enough to please them without committing him to anything.

Laish lay at the northern edge of the land, near one of the springs of the Jordan, below Mount Hermon. It is described as living like the Sidonians, the people of the Phoenician coast, perhaps a peaceful trading town. It was far from Sidon and had no allies. That made it an easy target.

The scouts' report uses the very language of the conquest under Joshua: the land is good, God has given it into your hand. But nothing in the story says God gave this command.
passages.later:
The scouts echo the spies of the wilderness, whom God himself told Moses to send: “Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites” (Numbers 13:2).

The book of Joshua mentions Dan's move north in a single sentence: “Later, when the territory of the Danites was lost to them, they went up and fought against Leshem, captured it, and put it to the sword” (Joshua 19:47).
passages.asks: The Danites asked a hired priest for a word from God and got the answer they wanted. Ask whether you look for guidance from people who will tell you what you hope to hear. And ask how you can tell the difference between God's leading and your own plans dressed in the language of faith.

passages.happening:
Six hundred armed men of Dan set out (verse 11). On the way they come to Micah's house, and the scouts tell them it has an ephod, household gods, a carved image and a cast idol. ‘Now think about what you should do’ (verse 14).

While the six hundred stand armed at the gate, the five go in and take the idol, the ephod and the household gods (verses 16-17). The priest asks what they are doing. They tell him to keep quiet. “Is it better for you to be a priest for the house of one person or a priest for a tribe and family in Israel?” (verse 19). ‘So the priest was glad’, and he goes with them, carrying the sacred things (verse 20).

They put their children, their animals and their goods in front and go on (verse 21). Micah and his neighbors chase after them. The Danites ask what is wrong with him. “You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have?” (verse 24). They warn him that angry men may kill him and his family. Micah sees they are too strong, and he turns back home (verses 25-26).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 17 ended with Micah sure that the LORD would be good to him because he had a Levite. Here stronger men simply carry off his gods and his priest.

The narrator lists the sacred objects again and again: the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, the cast idol. The repetition keeps the reader's eye on what these people trusted, and shows how empty it was. Gods that can be stolen cannot save anyone.

The priest is glad. He trades a post in one household for a post with a whole tribe. He serves whoever offers the better place.

Putting the families and animals in front was a sensible choice, to protect them from anyone chasing from behind.

Micah's cry is almost absurd, and it is also sad. ‘You took the gods I had made’. He made them, and now he has nothing. He has no one to appeal to, like so many people in these chapters. The rule of the strong decides everything.
passages.later: The prophets mocked gods that have to be carried: “Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch, their idols cannot speak. They must be carried because they cannot walk” (Jeremiah 10:5). Isaiah pictured a man who carves a god from the same wood he cooks with, and then prays to it, “Save me, for you are my god” (Isaiah 44:17).
passages.asks: Micah asked, ‘What else do I have?’ when his gods were taken. Ask what you rely on that could be taken from you in a single afternoon. And look at the glad priest. Ask whether any part of your service to God is shaped more by the offer of a bigger place than by his call.

passages.t: Laish destroyed, and an idol at Dan
passages.happening:
The Danites come to Laish, ‘to a tranquil and unsuspecting people, and they struck them with their swords and burned down the city’ (verse 27). No one rescues them, because they are far from Sidon and have no allies (verse 28).

The Danites rebuild the city and name it Dan, after their ancestor (verses 28-29). They set up the idol there. Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons serve as priests for the tribe of Dan ‘until the day of the captivity of the land’ (verse 30). Micah's idol stays there all the time that the house of God is at Shiloh (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Dan's move north is the last conquest in Judges. It has all the outward forms of Joshua's conquest: spies, a report that the land is good, a word about God giving it, and a city struck with the sword. What it lacks is any command from the LORD and any word about the town's wickedness. The narrator twice calls Laish tranquil and unsuspecting, and says there was no one to save them. That emphasis is itself his judgment.

The priest is named at last, and the name is a shock. He is Jonathan, a grandson of Moses. In the traditional Hebrew text a small raised letter changes Moses to Manasseh, probably to spare Moses the shame of an idol-serving grandson. Most translations read Moses.

‘The captivity of the land’ most likely means the Assyrian deportation of northern Israel, which began around 733 or 732 BC. Others think it means an earlier disaster, such as the Philistine capture of the ark and the loss of Shiloh in Samuel's day, which would fit the next verse.

Dan became the northern limit of the land. Its excavations have uncovered an Iron Age city with a large platform for worship, and centuries later King Jeroboam set up one of his golden calves there. The city stayed a center of worship the law did not allow.

The chapter ends by setting two places side by side: the idol at Dan and the house of God at Shiloh. One was false, and one was true.
passages.later:
Jeroboam later made Dan a center of false worship for the whole northern kingdom: “One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan. And this thing became a sin” (1 Kings 12:29-30).

The end of Shiloh's days as the place of God's house came in Samuel's time, when the Philistines defeated Israel and “The ark of God was captured” (1 Samuel 4:11).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible record the destruction of a peaceful town without a word of condemnation?

The condemnation is in the telling. The narrator calls Laish quiet and unsuspecting twice, and says there was no one to save them. The conquest under Joshua was presented as God's judgment on the wickedness of the peoples of Canaan. Here there is no mention of any sin in Laish and no word from the LORD, only a hired priest's vague assurance. Most readers take the story as a deliberate contrast with Joshua's conquest: the forms are the same, but the substance is not.

Judges often lets the facts speak without explicit comment, and in these last chapters it presents events as evidence of what Israel had become when everyone did what was right in his own eyes. A reader is meant to be disturbed.

This story gives no one any warrant for taking land or harming a people. It names a town that passed away long ago, and it says nothing about any nation, land or conflict of today. Nothing here permits contempt for the people of Laish or for anyone.
passages.asks: The Danites used the words of faith for something God had not commanded, and they succeeded. Ask whether you have ever taken success as proof that God approved. And ask who in your world is tranquil and unsuspecting, with no one to defend them, and what you owe them.
